name: San Martín Itunyoso Triqui
confidence_why: 6 independent first-hand sources agree (3 agree, 2 refine), none contradicts

audit.action: a better source should be cited for the same classification
audit.quote_check: confirmed in the copy we hold
audit.reasoning: Coding 'fixed-dominant, final syllable' (final stress) rests on DiCanio 2010 JIPA, an instrumental phonology article by the language's sole modern describer; the quotation is verbatim at pp.234 and 236 of the PDF downloaded now from the author's open site. The 2008 Berkeley dissertation (295 pp, Glottolog's top-ranked phonology for this languoid) says the same at p.20 ('having both final stress and a rich tone inventory'), and DiCanio 2014 and 2022 restate it as 'stem-final'/'root-final' stress with final-syllable lengthening independent of utterance position and focus. Nothing found contradicts the classification. Housekeeping only: the record has we have no copy, empty loc and empty grade and domain=not yet coded; register the downloaded JIPA PDF as held with loc pp.234-236, add dissertation p.20 as a corroborating source, set an strength of the evidence, and code the domain as root/stem-final (pronominal encliti

sources.citation: DiCanio 2010, Illustrations of the IPA: Itunyoso Trique, JIPA 40(2) (PDF from acsu.buffalo.edu/~cdicanio/pdfs/, read in full)
sources.quote: there are phonetic correlates to the final syllable prominence. Consonants and vowels in final syllables are noticeably longer [...] Since this is the position of stress in Trique [...] they result from a system of final prominence independent from tone.

sources.citation: DiCanio, Christian Thomas. 2008. The Phonetics and Phonology of San Martín Itunyoso Trique. PhD dissertation, University of California, Berkeley. 295 pp.
sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request)
sources.quote: p.20: 'Itunyoso Trique is prosodically complex, having both final stress and a rich tone inventory (9 tones). There are strong motivations for positing stress in the language apart from tone. The main evidence is the many asymmetries in the distribution of tone, consonants, and vowels... While word-final syllables license all segmental and autosegmental contrasts in the language, penultimate and antepenultimate syllables permit far fewer contrasts.' p.30: 'The similar patterns among the three dialects suggest that final stress is a shared feature in the Trique languages.'
sources.note: The only full phonology of the language (Glottolog listed by Glottolog as a phonology, 295 pp); §2.2 p.20 states final stress and gives the distributional evidence behind the JIPA summary; second independent locator for the record.

sources.citation: DiCanio, Christian. 2022. The evolution of tonally conditioned allomorphy in Triqui: evidence from spontaneous speech corpora. Linguistics Vanguard (aop). doi:10.1515/lingvan-2021-0093 (author preprint)
sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request)
sources.quote: 'Root-final syllables are accentually prominent and many phonological contrasts may only occur in this position... In addition, root-final syllables are phonetically longer than non-final syllables regardless of the position of the word in the utterance or focus condition (DiCanio 2010; DiCanio and Hatcher 2018).' Later: 'since stem-final syllables are stressed and carry heavy functional load in the language, stem-final syllables are often phonologically stable.'
sources.note: States the stress domain explicitly (root-/stem-final, enclitics outside; lengthening independent of utterance position and focus) -- fills the record's not yet coded domain field.

sources.citation: DiCanio, Christian & Ryan Bennett. 2018 (preprint; published 2020 in Gussenhoven & Chen eds., The Oxford Handbook of Language Prosody). Prosody in Mesoamerican languages.
sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request)
sources.quote: 'stress has been explored instrumentally in a few Mixtecan languages (Ixpantepec Nieves Mixtec (Carroll 2015), Southeastern Nochixtlán Mixtec (McKendry 2013), and Itunyoso Triqui (DiCanio 2008; 2010)). In each of these languages, the main correlate of stress is acoustic duration.'

sources.citation: DiCanio, Christian. 2014. Triqui tonal coarticulation and contrast preservation in tonal phonology. Proceedings of the Workshop on the Sound Systems of Mexico and Central America (SSMCA), Yale. (author PDF)
sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request)
sources.quote: 'In addition to lexical tone, IT possesses stem-final stress. Final syllables are phonetically longer than non-final syllables and more phonological contrasts are realized on final syllables as well (DiCanio, 2008, 2010).'
sources.note: One-line restatement 'IT possesses stem-final stress' with duration evidence; corroborates domain = stem.

sources.citation: DiCanio, Christian T. 2010. Illustrations of the IPA: Itunyoso Trique. Journal of the International Phonetic Association 40(2):227-238. doi:10.1017/S0025100310000034
sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request)
sources.quote: 'Apart from distributional asymmetries in segment types and tone, there are phonetic correlates to the final syllable prominence. Consonants and vowels in final syllables are noticeably longer than those occurring in non-final syllables.' (p.234) ... 'Since this is the position of stress in Trique, such lengthening can be considered a type of prosodic strengthening' ... 'they result from a system of final prominence independent from tone.' (p.236)
sources.note: The deciding source itself was not registered as held (we have no copy); now obtained by the project so the record can carry a locator (pp.234-236) and an strength of the evidence.
